title: Angı 2021 — music form and movement
text: The study examines musical characteristics of The Skeleton Dance and the relationship between musical form and movement. It describes the cartoon as an example where music was composed before images and animation was shaped around musical structure. The author discusses potential educational use for listening, analysis/grouping, and practical activities. This is a descriptive study; do not treat it as a quantitative motion-capture experiment.

title: Benner 2022 — dancing skeletons, materiality, and music
text: The chapter discusses Disney's dancing-skeleton films beginning with The Skeleton Dance (1929). Skeletons are framed as animated performers, musicians, and toy-like playable bodies. Their visual and acoustic qualities make animation's possibilities visible; the films also emphasize bone sounds and musical practices. Use this as a cultural/film-studies perspective, distinct from computational pose analysis.

title: Hernández Polo 2013 — Silly Symphonies as audiovisual education
text: The article introduces Walt Disney's Silly Symphonies from a didactic and motivational perspective. It describes The Skeleton Dance (1929) as the first short in the series and highlights synchronization between music, movement, image expression, and feeling as a central production concern. It proposes the shorts as resources for recognizing musical language and animation history. Treat these as claims summarized from a repository record, pending full-text review.

title: Wang and Sutrisno 2026 — temporal segmentation of dance skeletons
text: The paper evaluates video-derived skeleton sequences for temporal action segmentation in continuous dance. It compares BODY-25 and COCO-18 pose representations and FACT versus MS-TCN++ temporal models under a unified protocol. The abstract reports that FACT achieved stronger segment-level F1/Edit performance and BODY-25 generally outperformed COCO-18 in their experiments. These results are dataset/protocol-specific and should not be generalized to The Skeleton Dance without evaluation.

title: Dance pose classification from motion capture
text: This article compares classifiers for identifying dance poses from motion-capture data. It is relevant to designing a baseline that classifies normalized pose features and to evaluating alternatives rather than assuming a single classifier is best. The present seed note does not include classifier names or quantitative results; consult the paper before selecting a method.

title: Papatheodorou and Wolpert 2023 — embodied search through dance poses
text: The paper describes an interactive installation that uses camera-based skeleton tracking and a pose/film indexing system to retrieve matching short film clips from body poses. It provides a precedent for searching a film corpus through embodied pose similarity, and for connecting skeleton tracking with cultural-media archives. It is not specifically a study of The Skeleton Dance.

title: Shiratori, Nakazawa, and Ikeuchi 2006 — dance motion matched to music
text: The method analyzes motion and music separately, deriving motion features from rhythm and intensity and music features from rhythm, structure, and intensity. Candidate motion segments are matched to music segments by rhythm and then intensity, with animator control over segment assignments. This motivates separating measurable timing/intensity features from higher-level semantic labels in the prototype.

title: Nguyen et al. 2025 — music-driven dance motion estimation
text: The ICCV 2025 paper studies joint use of music and video for dance motion estimation, including a large egocentric dance dataset and a Skeleton Mamba architecture for sequence modeling. The abstract reports improvements over compared methods. For this project, it is a recent reference for modeling temporal skeleton structure alongside music, but its egocentric setting differs from a 1929 hand-drawn cartoon.

title: Mu 2022 — pose-estimation-assisted dance tracking
text: The article describes extracting dance skeleton keypoint coordinates from video and using music-related features in a dance-motion generation system. It is relevant to a video-to-keypoints pipeline, but exact implementation details and reported performance must be checked in the full article before adoption.

title: Skeleton Dance project hypothesis — not a published finding
text: Proposed prototype: represent X as pose/form, Y as motion dynamics/intensity, and Z as time/rhythm, while keeping measured numeric features separate from interpretive semantic labels. Start with video-derived pose/keypoint sequences, preserve timestamps and confidence values, then compare motion events against audio beat/structure. This is a project design hypothesis inspired by the indexed literature, not a finding established by those papers.
